column3: It directly depicts a group unable to help someone apart from God, and the person's failure to save himself.
It traces deviation through inherited excess and following those already astray, supplying a social route into lost guidance.
The Day of Gathering separates responsibility for misleading from self-incurred loss of the path.
The immediately preceding verse pairs divine misguidance with no protector and no route back after punishment is seen.
It warns before an irrevocable day when neither refuge nor denial remains, extending the focus's closed-path horizon.
It directly denies any protector or helper apart from God, though it does not state the loss of a path.
It joins God's sufficiency with the formula that one He leaves astray has no guide.
It makes present blindness persist into the Hereafter as a condition of being further astray from the way.
God's dominion grounds the denial of any protector or helper apart from Him, but this repeats the support theme.
Attachment to wrongdoers leads to the Fire and leaves no protectors or help, adding a moral cause for abandonment.
The distribution of children and barrenness does not clarify lost guidance or unavailable support.
Its account of people seeking to mislead others concerns reciprocal self-harm, not the focus's final lack of path or aid.
Qarun's collapse shows both a supporting faction and self-rescue failing apart from God.
Different inward dispositions issue in differently guided ways, but it adds little to the focus's closure of the way.
Life and death under divine dominion frame the repeated denial of protectors and helpers.
It explicitly says that for one God has left astray no path can be found, while tying the condition to what was earned.
God's creative gift of children has no material connection to the focus's two claims.
It identifies associating partners as a means of leading people from God's way, but lacks the focus's support and closure language.
It combines intensified punishment with no protectors apart from God, giving an eschatological setting for failed support.
The invitation to a way of right conduct is a positive counterpart, but it does not illuminate why no way remains in the focus.
Following desire without knowledge results in misguidance and no helper, though earlier cards state the pattern more directly.
It combines divine misguidance, no protectors apart from God, gathering, and Hell, giving the focus a concrete final outcome.
Dispute over the Hour is called far error, but this contrast evidence does not explain the focus's no-path formula.
The denial of protector and intercessor apart from God supports the exclusive-help theme, but is now redundant.
Accountability, false partners, being barred from the way, and no guide form a broad parallel already covered more directly.
Calling adultery an evil way uses path language in a different ethical setting.
The test of a claimed special friendship with God does not clarify unavailable aid or guidance.
It portrays promised human aid failing under pressure, a worldly analogy weaker than the direct theological formulations.
Stillness of ships in wind does not add to the focus's guidance or support themes.
Those invoked apart from God cannot aid their followers or themselves, sharply illustrating the incapacity of alternative helpers.
Military preparation and spending in God's cause do not clarify the focus's lost path or absent protectors.
People in punishment blame their leaders for leading them astray, adding human mediation to the origin of path-loss.
Blocking others from God's way supplies a general mechanism of deviation, but not the focus's final condition.
The accounting of hardship in striving does not clarify the focus's themes.
It contrasts chosen protectors with God as the true Protector who gives life to the dead, closely reinforcing the surah context.
Joseph's brothers calling their father mistaken is a local family judgment, not the relevant kind of misguidance.
Rules about alliance and conflict with defectors do not explain the focus's theological denial of aid.
Provision for emigrants who die concerns reward, not a lost route or unavailable support.
God's knowledge of who strays and who is guided states the distinction without adding the focus's consequences.
The service of jinn under Solomon and God's guarding them is unrelated.
It places those taking protectors apart from God under God's watch, furnishing nearby context for the focus's denial of such protectors.
The challenge, 'Why do you not help one another?', gives a stark judgment-scene instance of help's total failure.
The contrast between fighting for God and for false powers concerns allegiance in conflict, not the focus's final lack of a path.
It shows agents who block people from the way while the blocked imagine themselves guided, clarifying deceptive path-loss.
The rhetorical question exposes the delusion that any army can help against the Merciful.
On the day of flight there is no protector from God, followed by the same formula that the misled have no guide.
Earthly paths made for guidance form a distant positive counterpart to the denied path in the focus.
It affirms that one may take a way to the Lord, serving as a limited contrast to the focus's no-way condition.
After drowning and entering the Fire, they find no helpers apart from God, closely joining punishment and failed support.
It depicts wrongdoers fearing the inevitable result of what they earned, contextualizing the focus's judicial outcome.
Those gathered face-down toward Hell are in the worst place and farthest from the way, giving an eschatological embodiment of path-loss.
The inverse claim that none can mislead one God guides adds little after the direct no-guide formulations.
The opponents' secret claim that the messenger is enchanted does not clarify the focus.
The bare assurance of divine support lacks a relevant connection beyond the shared help root.
Taking devils as protectors while thinking oneself guided explicitly links false allegiance to mistaken guidance.
It directly says wrongdoers have neither protector nor helper, adding the surah's mercy-and-justice frame.
God's knowledge of the astray and guided repeats an already established distinction without the focus's closing imagery.
The supposed deities fail to help and disappear from their worshippers, a concrete collapse of alternative protectors.
Wealth and splendor being used to lead from God's way adds a specific worldly instrument of deviation.
The prohibited marriage practice being an evil way is not relevant to the focus's path of guidance.
Refusing God's caller leaves no escape and no protectors apart from Him, then names the condition clear misguidance.
God as Protector who spreads mercy after despair is a nearby positive counterpart, but not the focus's condition.
Disbelief combined with blocking God's way results in far error, but it is less direct than prior path-loss cards.
The questioned false gods can neither help their followers nor defend themselves, reinforcing the failure of alternatives.
Additional punishment for those who block God's way adds consequence but repeats a cause already supplied.
The comparison of religious services and striving does not explain the lack of a viable path or helper.
It tersely denies both personal power and any helper, a compact parallel to the focus's failed support.
Its warning of the Day of Gathering and division between Garden and Blaze supplies the surah's final-judgment setting.
On that day no close associate benefits another and none are helped, specifying the collapse of reciprocal support.
No one can protect against God's harm or mercy, and no protector or helper exists apart from Him; the formula is now redundant.
In the Fire, regret over disobeying God and the messenger gives an experiential consequence of having followed a wrong way.
God as sufficient guide and helper amid prophetic opposition is a positive counterpart rather than an explanation of the focus.
Those struck with punishment neither submit nor plead, offering a limited behavioral contrast to any turn back.
Leading others from God's way brings disgrace and burning punishment, but repeats the deviation-to-punishment pattern.
Moses's conflict and its attribution to a manifestly misleading enemy is too narrative-specific to clarify the focus.
God guides by the Book and leaves no guide for whom He misguides, but earlier cards state this more tightly.
Physical broad roads are not the moral or judicial path at issue in the focus.
The command to fight in God's way does not add to the focus's no-path or no-helper claim.
No one can repel God's intended harm and there is no protector apart from Him, a related but redundant formulation.
The hypothetical path sought by alleged gods concerns divine hierarchy, not the condemned person's lack of guidance.
No escape and no protector or helper apart from God restate the support theme without the focus's path language.
The regulation of alliances among people does not explain the focus's eschatological lack of protectors.
The declaration of God's transcendence adds no distinct guidance or support content.
Eternal residence without any protector or helper gives the strongest finality to the focus's failed-support claim.
The declaration that punishment has no repeller gives a concise parallel to the irreversible consequence behind the focus.
Oaths used as a shield become a means of blocking God's way, a secondary mechanism of deviation.
The claimed absence of obligation toward outsiders uses 'way' in a legal sense unrelated to guidance.
When God's command arrives, invoked gods bring no benefit and only increase ruin, a concrete failure of false support.
The generic statement of a sign for believers has no relevant content by itself.
A prophet's request for help against corrupters does not explain the focus's final absence of help.
The inability to possess anything against God's trial gives a distant parallel to divine decisiveness, but not the focus's core terms.
A messenger's denial of personal error is not informative about the focus's condition of misguidance.
A town's loss of security and provision after ingratitude does not clarify absent protectors or a closed path.
The messenger cannot guide the blind away from their error, a partial parallel to the focus's no-path consequence.
Hard hearts and signs in stones do not materially clarify the focus's support or path themes.
The promise of divine help and near victory is a positive assurance, not the focus's condition of unavailable aid.
Household etiquette and marital restrictions do not connect to the focus's themes.
Being farther from the even way describes punishment and error, but adds little after stronger eschatological parallels.
Rules for nursing, provision, and consultation are unrelated.
Disobeying God's and the messenger's decision is called clear error, a general cause but not the focus's final condition.
The adjacent verse shows the wrongdoers exposed to the punishment in humiliation, completing the immediate judgment scene of the focus.
It combines the exact claim that one God leaves astray has no guide with the denial that such people have helpers.
It directly states that for one God sends astray there is no guide and depicts them wandering blindly.
It directly says that one God leaves astray will never find a guiding protector.
After God causes a follower of desire to stray, it asks who could guide him after God, clarifying the finality of the focus's no-path claim.
It joins recompense for evil with having no protector or helper apart from God.
It links entry into the Fire with disgrace and the absence of any helpers for wrongdoers.
The nullification of deeds in this world and the next is paired with having no helpers.
It makes divine rejection decisive by stating that one God curses will find no helper.
The lowest level of the Fire is paired with the declaration that no helper will be found for hypocrites.
It places punishment for refusal alongside the lack of any protector or helper apart from God.
The warning of gathering before God specifies that there will be no protector or intercessor apart from Him.
It describes a soul held by what it earned, without any protector or intercessor, in a judgment setting.
The false objects of devotion can neither help their followers nor help themselves, closely paralleling failed alternative support.
No one can remove harm God decrees, which reinforces the focus's denial of independent rescue.
It pairs punishment in both worlds with the statement that they have no protector from God.
Those invoked apart from God cannot remove or redirect harm, defining the practical failure of alternative recourse.
In danger at sea, all invoked beings apart from God disappear from view, exposing the collapse of false reliance.
God has no partner in His judgment and takes no protector into it, grounding the exclusivity assumed by the focus.
It challenges the claim that anyone can protect people from the Merciful, directly testing the premise of alternative protection.
It calls the invoked object an evil protector and evil helper, a concise contrary diagnosis of false allegiance.
God protects while none can be protected against Him, giving a direct sovereignty rationale for the focus's failed helpers.
Objects taken as gods apart from God possess neither harm nor benefit, death, life, or resurrection.
When alleged partners are summoned, they do not answer; the scene concretizes the abandonment of their devotees.
The associates will have no intercessors among their alleged partners, extending the breakdown of support at judgment.
Those invoked apart from God possess nothing, share no authority, and provide no supporting aid.
If the Merciful intends harm, the intercession of other gods brings no benefit and they cannot save.
The gods taken apart from God cannot help their worshippers, despite being treated as a supporting host.
The challenge about whether invoked beings can remove God's harm directly contests their claimed protective power.
The question about taking intercessors apart from God exposes reliance on beings lacking independent authority.
All intercession belongs to God, giving the positive ground for why no independent intercessory support remains.
On the approaching Day, wrongdoers have neither a devoted friend nor an intercessor whose plea is received.
The inhabitants of the Fire tell one another that none can lessen the punishment, showing the exhaustion of all mutual aid.
